extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy/psychology of humor; general readers interested in theories and ethics of humor
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying philosophical and psychological criteria for what counts as humor, why laughter occurs, and ethical/social considerations in producing or evaluating humorous content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity between concept and reality
rubrics_metrics.description: “The cause of laughter in every case is simply the sudden perception of the incongruity between a concept and the real objects which have been thought through it in some relation, and laughter itself is just the expression of this incongruity.” (Schopenhauer)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor arises when an abstract idea or expectation is suddenly shown to mismatch the real object or situation; examples include the prison-guard/convict anecdote and the Austrian walking joke. Producing such incongruity often requires setting up a general conception and then revealing a case that violates it. Anti-pattern: no clear mismatch or the audience cannot perceive the conceptual switch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit as facility to subsume disparate items under an abstract conception
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit “consists entirely in a facility for finding for every object that appears a conception under which it certainly can be thought, though it is very different from all the other objects which come under this conception.” (Schopenhauer)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creative use of abstract categories that can (mis)apply to very different things makes for witty material. Example guidance: construct a general rule and then show a borderline or excluded case that nevertheless fits. Anti-pattern: forced or opaque conceptual mappings that audiences cannot follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offensiveness of being laughed at (incongruity as insult)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter directed at a person can offend because it asserts a great incongruity between their conceptions and objective realities; 'ludicrous' or 'absurd' can be insulting. (Schopenhauer)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When humor targets a person’s beliefs or identity, it can function as a public announcement of their error or inadequacy. Evaluate ethical risks: such laughter may humiliate or demean. Consider performer-audience relationship, power differentials, and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure from the victory of perception over thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter can stem from the pleasure of perception (which requires no exertion) 'winning' over effortful thought; perception is immediate and answers for itself, while thinking requires exertion (Schopenhauer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor that foregrounds a simple perceptual insight undermining complicated thought can produce delight. This helps explain why simple visual or situational reveals can be funny. Anti-pattern: jokes that require excessive cognitive work without payoff feel laborious rather than amusing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity-resolution (enjoyment of fitting anomaly into schema)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporary psychologists (e.g., Thomas Schultz, Jerry Suls) argue that amusement often comes from resolving an apparent anomaly by fitting it into a conceptual schema; unresolvable incongruity is 'nonsense.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective jokes often create a temporary cognitive problem that the audience 'solves' (e.g., puns, double meanings like Mae West's 'institution' quip). Craft punch lines so that the reinterpretation of prior material is attainable and rewarding. Anti-pattern: unresolved ambiguity that leaves listeners confused rather than amused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception + enjoyment + intrinsic enjoyment (Michael Clark's three conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor requires (1) perception (thinking/imagining) of an object as incongruous, (2) enjoyment of perceiving it, and (3) enjoyment of the incongruity at least partly for its own sake rather than solely for an ulterior reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a checklist: (a) make incongruity perceivable, (b) shape performance to elicit pleasure, (c) ensure the pleasure is not only instrumental (e.g., not only a social payoff). If any of the three is missing, the material may fail to be experienced as humorous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of overriding negative emotions
rubrics_metrics.description: Perception of incongruity is not sufficient for laughter when the perception is accompanied by stronger emotions (fear, pity, moral disapproval, indignation, disgust) that block risible amusement (James Beattie).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess context and stakes: if the incongruity evokes a more powerful aversive emotion, humor will likely fail or be inappropriate. Example: a dangerous or tragic mismatch will produce fear or pity instead of laughter. When crafting humor, avoid triggering dominant negative emotions if the goal is amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish humorous enjoyment from other aesthetic enjoyments
rubrics_metrics.description: Some violations of expectation produce non-humorous aesthetic pleasures (grotesque, macabre, horrible, bizarre, fantastic) rather than amusement (Morreall; examples from Sophocles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating humor, check whether the audience’s enjoyment is genuinely amusement (laughter/pleasure) rather than fascination, horror, or pity. This helps classify material and choose suitable techniques for comedic versus other artistic aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor as play and laughter as play signal
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor can be analyzed as a kind of play; laughter and smiling evolved as play signals to mark non-serious mock-aggression and to distinguish playful activity from real threat (ethologists, van Hooff, Eastman).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat comedic interactions as play: create safe, non-threatening violations of expectations. Use clear play signals (tone, smile, exaggerated behavior) so participants know the activity is non-serious. Anti-pattern: ambiguous signaling that causes participants to take the play literally and respond defensively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Playfulness as a virtue (eutrapelia) — right time, place, and degree
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle and Aquinas: there is a virtue of ready-wittedness or appropriate playfulness (eutrapelia); excess (vulgar buffoonery) and deficiency (boorishness) are vices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate humor for moderation: is it appropriate to context and audience? Aim for a balance—engaging and agreeable without excess. Consider social norms and occasions to avoid buffoonery or being a kill-joy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play signals (facial/vocal markers) distinguish humor from aggression
rubrics_metrics.description: Evolutionary/ethological markers—'silent bared-teeth' social grimace evolved into human smile; 'relaxed open-mouth display' and staccato out-breathing evolved into laughter—signal that mock-aggression is play, not real attack (van Hooff).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performers should use recognizable facial and vocal cues to indicate playfulness. In writing, stage directions, tone markers, or context can serve analogous signaling. Mis-signaling can escalate into real conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Violation of Gricean conversational maxims as a comic technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor often arises from deliberately breaking conversational rules (Grice): (1) Do not say what you believe to be false; (2) Do not say that for which you lack adequate evidence; (3) Avoid obscurity; (4) Avoid ambiguity; (5) Be brief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each maxim can be exploited: lie/exaggerate for effect (Rule 1), present fantasy as fact (Rule 2), use evasive or obscure replies for comic effect (Rule 3), switch interpretations at the punch line (Rule 4), and over-extend a complaint into rant for catharsis (Rule 5). Use deliberate violations consciously; anti-pattern: opaque violations that the audience can't decode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social amplification of laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter is overwhelmingly social — we are far more likely to laugh with others than alone (estimate: ~30x) — and laughter evolved as a social/play signal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design performance and delivery to leverage social dynamics: audience interaction, timing with others’ laughter, and communal contexts enhance funniness. Solo delivery (e.g., written joke) may need stronger cues to elicit similar responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor as social lubricant and instrument of critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor can foster tolerance for ambiguity/diversity, promote creative problem-solving, engender trust, reduce conflict, and serve as a vehicle for critical analysis, exposing social realities and telling truth to power (Ted Cohen; APA handbook).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use humor strategically to ease negative emotions in difficult communications (apologies, criticisms, warnings) or to make critique palatable. Example: a comedic twist in a debt-collection letter can defuse hostility. Anti-pattern: humor that trivializes serious issues or undermines necessary accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical assessment of stereotype-based jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: Playing with negative stereotypes in jokes does not necessarily indicate endorsement, but it keeps stereotypes in circulation and can be harmful in cultures where they support prejudice and injustice (discussion of Polish jokes, Davies, Anderson, Horisk).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether stereotype-based humor perpetuates harm: consider cultural context, audience composition, performer intent, and potential for reinforcing prejudice. Even if a joke is 'playful', its social effect may be negative; prefer techniques that punch up or subvert rather than reinforce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral impact of immorality in humor (comic moralism vs immoralism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophical debate over whether immoral elements in humor reduce funniness (comic moralism), always enhance it (comic immoralism), or sometimes affect it (moderate comic moralism). Familiarity with offensive cycles can change audience response (e.g., Dead Baby jokes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess audience familiarity and tolerance: shock/immorality may increase amusement for some in-group audiences but will offend others. Use moral considerations as part of aesthetic evaluation; be mindful that context dramatically changes effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between comic and tragic contradictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Kierkegaard/Aristotle: both tragedy and comedy are based on contradiction, but the tragic is the 'suffering contradiction' while the comic is the 'painless contradiction'—the comic apprehension makes a way out or renders the contradiction harmless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When crafting comedic material involving contradictions, ensure the audience perceives the contradiction as non-destructive or viewable from a safe perspective. If the contradiction evokes despair or irreversible harm, it will read as tragic, not comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Features of comedy as a genre (anti-heroic, pragmatic, egalitarian)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy embodies an anti-heroic, pragmatic attitude: methods include deal-making, trickery, getting an enemy drunk, running away; it elevates ordinary people, families, and groups, uses common speech, and values cleverness/adaptability over warrior virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate or produce comedic works by checking for these features: focus on group/family, use of everyday language, anti-elitist protagonists, and solutions based on cunning rather than heroic sacrifice. Anti-pattern: elevating comedy to tragic form by using elevated diction or heroic solitary protagonists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor fosters abstract distancing and rational perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor enables a nonpractical, less self-centered frame that allows abstract thinking—viewing personal mishaps from a broader perspective and thereby aiding rationality and objectivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use distancing, reframing, and universalizing details to turn personal mishaps into material that invites reflective amusement rather than shame or anger. Avoid humor in contexts where immediate practical action is required (dangerous situations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiological and psychological health benefits of laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter reduces stress (lowers epinephrine, norepinephrine, cortisol), decreases muscle tension, heart rate, blood pressure, increases pain tolerance and immune activity, and provides psychological 'rest' (research cited: Martin et al., Morreall).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When justifying or evaluating humor's value, include health benefits as positive outcomes. Consider these benefits when advocating for humor in therapeutic, workplace, or educational settings. Avoid using humor in ways that would trigger stress or humiliation, which can negate benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standup comedy features overlapping with philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: Standup shares at least seven affinities with philosophy: conversational format, reflection on familiar/puzzling experiences, starting from a puzzling 'X—what's up with that?', emotional disengagement, and critical thinking (first five listed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For standup writing/analysis: favor conversational tone, choose relatable puzzling observations, frame material as probing questions, maintain a measured emotional stance, and highlight critical insight. These features help connect comedic content to broader reflective aims.
